name: Divisibility rules
formula: 3, 9: \text{ digit sum} \qquad 11: \text{ alternating digit sum} \qquad 4, 8: \text{ last } 2, 3 \text{ digits} \qquad 6 = 2 \cdot 3, \ 12 = 3 \cdot 4
whenToUse: Testing divisibility of a large number quickly, or finding a missing digit that makes a number divisible by something.
example: For $7392$: the alternating sum $2 - 9 + 3 - 7 = -11$ is a multiple of $11$, so $11 \mid 7392$. The digit sum $21$ is a multiple of $3$ but not $9$, and $92$ is a multiple of $4$, so $12 \mid 7392$ too.
pitfall: For a composite divisor, split it into COPRIME factors: test $12$ as $3$ and $4$, never as $2$ and $6$. Divisibility by $4$ and $8$ uses the last digits, not the digit sum.
derivation: Since $10 \equiv 1 \pmod 9$, every power of $10$ is $1$ modulo $9$ (and $3$), so a number is congruent to its digit sum. Since $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$, the powers alternate between $1$ and $-1$.
